scopeReview: SPS-2.B.1–2: changing education, work, health, contraception and social/political roles influence fertility, mortality and migration. Ravenstein treated as contextual historical tendencies, never biological restrictions. No stereotypes, individual prescriptions or universal fertility targets.
varietyReview: District association, migration sex shares, time-use composition and maternal mortality denominator; applied mechanisms cover schooling/marriage, voluntary spacing, independent migration, rural/urban barriers, representation and complementary care policies. All five skills, mixed difficulty and varied keys.
repetitionReview: New questions focus on changing women’s roles rather than repeating policy definitions. Cohort timing appears only as a mechanism for early childbearing, not a repeat of2.7 policy-tempo evaluation. Paid/unpaid composition and live-birth denominators introduce distinct quantitative reasoning.
referenceNote: Primary curriculum/institutional research and Ravenstein publication identity checked; original hypothetical numbers and scenarios. No historical quotations or real-country statistical claims copied. No third-party resources added to the student catalog; no independent human review claimed.

questions.correctOption: Higher completion percentages are associated with lower adolescent birth rates across these districts.
questions.independentReview: Sorted completion30/60/90 and paired rates80/50/20, confirming a strict inverse association. Denominators for counts and confounding variables are absent; no individual or causal conclusion is justified.

questions.correctOption: Women are 60% of internal migrants but 40% of international migrants in this sample.
questions.independentReview: Independently computed600/(600+400)=.6 and200/(200+300)=.4. Historical tendencies are context-dependent, not biological restrictions or claims that women cannot move internationally.

questions.correctOption: Equal total work time can coexist with a large difference in the division between paid work and unpaid care.
questions.independentReview: Summed4+6=10 and8+2=10; verified paid-hour gap4 and unpaid-care gap4 in opposite directions. Kept time allocation separate from wages, preferences and a causal explanation.

questions.correctOption: The ratio falls from 800 to 300 per 100,000 live births; the chart alone does not isolate the cause.
questions.independentReview: Independently scaled80/10000×100000=800 and30/10000×100000=300. Both periods use live births, not total residents. The inference is a measured ratio decline, not a treatment effect or medical recommendation.

questions.correctOption: Later marriage can delay first births and reduce exposure to early childbearing.
questions.independentReview: Checked the mechanism between continued schooling, marriage timing and early births against institutional research. Delayed first births are a conditional pathway, not proof of a fixed reduction in lifetime births or immediate population decline.

questions.correctOption: Greater ability to space or avoid unintended births in line with individual intentions.
questions.independentReview: Identified the direct mechanism of the specified voluntary service: enabling desired spacing/avoidance. Avoided universal fertility targets, medical instructions or claims that access alone guarantees zero unintended pregnancies.

questions.correctOption: Test them against changing opportunities and observed flows rather than treating them as permanent restrictions.
questions.independentReview: Used the supplied causal opportunity—direct skilled-job recruitment—to interpret changing female migration roles. Historical patterns do not logically prohibit new flows; no universal reversal or exclusion of male migration is inferred.

questions.correctOption: Compare rural and urban employment, care responsibilities and access to services.
questions.independentReview: Identified the missing within-country dimensions explicitly described: rural/urban location, transport and care. Disaggregated analysis avoids ecological inference while preserving variation within each category.

questions.correctOption: Greater influence over service priorities can improve access relevant to maternal survival.
questions.independentReview: Separated political agency, resource allocation and a potential mortality pathway. The question tests demographic mechanisms, not a medical prediction or a claim that political representation mechanically sets outcomes.

questions.correctOption: Employment conditions, care support, health access and social values can modify the relationship.
questions.independentReview: Held one national indicator similar while allowing other relevant conditions to differ. A multicausal interpretation explains nonidentical outcomes without dismissing education or imposing identical individual choices.

questions.correctOption: Reducing care constraints can support women’s employment and reproductive choices without requiring everyone to choose fewer births.
questions.independentReview: Checked the distinction between enabling choices and enforcing fewer births. Complementary work/care arrangements can relax constraints; no single fertility direction or guaranteed labor response is asserted.
